newsitem.title: UK: British families change living, buying habits.
newsitem.headline: British families change living, buying habits.

text.p: Britain has become a nation of smaller households, with more single-parent families and working mothers, according to a nationwide survey published on Thursday.
People are also better educated than they were 25 years ago and more own their own homes.

The General Household Survey by the Office for National Statistics (GHS) showed the standard of living has increased in the quarter century since the poll began with more people owning consumer goods ranging from CD players to microwave ovens and video recorders.
"This is the only national survey of data on certain topics," Nikki Bennett of the GHS told a press conference. "It helps to paint a picture of how society is changing."

The survey compiled responses from about 18,000 adults from 10,000 households questioned between April 1995 and March 1996. It showed that the mean household size has declined steadily from 2.91 people in 1971 to 2.4 people in 1995.

Married or cohabiting couples with no dependent children accounted for 36 percent of the population while people living alone rose from 17 percent in 1971 to 28 percent last year. Twenty-four percent of those questioned were couples with dependent children.

"The proportion of families with dependent children headed by lone parents increased threefold (eight to 22 percent) between 1971 and 1995. Over the same period the proportion headed by single (never married) mothers rose from one percent to eight percent," the GHS said.

The survey also indicated the economic pressures on many families, with a threefold increase in the number of working women with children under five years old, up from five percent in 1983 to 16 percent last year.
Women working part-time also doubled within the same period. But more people owned their own homes last year, 68 percent compared to just under one half in 1971.

The ethnic composition of Britain has changed little since 1983. Like then, two percent of the population was Indian, one percent was Pakistani/Bangladeshi and an equal number described themselves as black Caribbean.
The number of whites was 94 percent in 1995, which was offset by a one percent rise in the number of people classifed as "other ethnic groups", which totalled one percent in 1983.
For most women the pill was the favoured method of contraception (25 percent), followed by sterilisaton (24 percent) and the condom (18 percent)
